title: Concurrent Changes in Body Roundness Index and Grip Strength in Relation to Incident Disability: Do Changes Add Information Beyond Current Status?
content: Background/Objectives: Dynapenic abdominal obesity is associated with functional disability, but whether concurrent within-person changes in body roundness index (BRI) and grip strength are associated with later disability, and whether they add prognostic information beyond current measurements, remain uncertain. Methods: We studied 9,745 Health and Retirement Study participants aged 50 years or older with BRI and grip strength measured approximately four years apart. Sex-specific conditional changes defined four joint-change groups. Incident activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL) disability through 2022 were evaluated using cause-specific Cox models, competing-risk analyses, and nested prognostic models. Results: During a median follow-up of 4.2 years, 1,067 ADL and 1,026 IADL events occurred. Compared with favorable changes in both measures, concurrent greater-than-expected BRI gain and grip strength decline were associated with ADL disability (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.28; 95% confidence interval, 1.08–1.53) and IADL disability (1.24; 1.04–1.48), although the latter was borderline after multiplicity adjustment. Risks were not clearly higher than with grip strength decline alone (ADL, 1.12; 0.95–1.33). Adding change groups to models containing current BRI and grip strength did not improve model fit (ADL, P = 0.957; IADL, P = 0.479) or optimism-corrected discrimination. Conclusions: Concurrent adverse BRI and grip strength changes were associated with modestly higher disability risk than favorable changes. However, this pattern was not clearly distinguishable from grip strength decline alone and provided little additional prognostic information beyond current measurements.
